authors.name: Marcus Aurelius
authors.bio: Last of the Five Good Emperors. His private journal, the Meditations, is the most intimate record of Stoic practice we have.

authors.name: Seneca the Younger
authors.bio: Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman. His letters and essays on anger, time, and providence remain foundational Stoic reading.

authors.name: Epictetus
authors.bio: Born enslaved, later a celebrated teacher in Nicopolis. His Discourses and Enchiridion teach the dichotomy of control.

authors.name: Zeno of Citium
authors.bio: Merchant turned philosopher who founded Stoicism in Athens, teaching at the Painted Porch.

authors.name: Cleanthes
authors.bio: Second head of the Stoic school after Zeno. Known for his Hymn to Zeus and his teaching on fate and acceptance.

authors.name: Buddha
authors.bio: Siddhartha Gautama, whose teachings on suffering, mindfulness, and compassion shaped much of Asian thought.

authors.name: Confucius
authors.bio: Chinese teacher whose Analects shaped ethics, education, and government across East Asia for two thousand years.

authors.name: Lao Tzu
authors.bio: Traditionally credited with the Tao Te Ching, a short text on simplicity, nature, and effortless action.

authors.name: William Shakespeare
authors.bio: English playwright and poet whose plays and sonnets remain among the most quoted works in English.

authors.name: Aristotle
authors.bio: Student of Plato and teacher of Alexander. His works cover logic, ethics, politics, and natural science.

authors.name: Plato
authors.bio: Student of Socrates and founder of the Academy. His dialogues shaped Western philosophy.

authors.name: Socrates
authors.bio: Athenian philosopher known through Plato's dialogues. He taught by questioning and lived by examined principles.

authors.name: Heraclitus
authors.bio: Presocratic philosopher of change and flux, known for the image of the ever-changing river.

authors.name: Diogenes
authors.bio: Cynic philosopher famous for radical simplicity, frank speech, and living in a barrel in Corinth.

authors.name: Cicero
authors.bio: Roman orator and statesman whose letters and treatises carried Greek philosophy into Latin.

authors.name: Aesop
authors.bio: Traditionally credited with the fables that teach practical wisdom through short animal stories.

blogs.title: The Dichotomy of Control: The One Idea That Changes Everything
blogs.excerpt: Some things are up to us, and some things are not. Learning to tell the difference is the whole game.
blogs.content:
# The Dichotomy of Control

Epictetus opens the Enchiridion with a line that still cuts through noise two thousand years later: some things are up to us, and some things are not.

## What is up to us

Our judgements. Our impulses. Our desires and aversions. In short: the way we respond.

## What is not up to us

Our body. Our property. Our reputation. Our job. In short: everything outside our own mind.

## Why it matters

Most suffering comes from demanding control over the second list while neglecting the first. You cannot control the traffic, the market, or what someone thinks of you. You can control whether you answer with patience or with anger.

## A daily practice

Each morning, write two columns: "Up to me" and "Not up to me". Put the day's worries in the right column. Act on the first. Release the second.

That is the whole practice. It takes a minute, and it changes the day.
blogs.seoDescription: Some things are up to us, some are not. A plain guide to Epictetus and daily practice.

blogs.title: Memento Mori: Remember You Will Die (And Why That Is Good News)
blogs.excerpt: Remembering death is not morbid. It is the fastest way to stop wasting time.
blogs.content:
# Memento Mori

The Stoics kept death close — not to frighten themselves, but to focus themselves.

## The point

If this day were your last, would you spend it arguing online, or calling someone you love? Memento mori asks that question before the day is spent.

## Seneca on time

Seneca wrote that we are not given a short life — we waste much of it. We spend time as if it were unlimited, then panic when it runs out.

## A gentle practice

Once a day, pause and say: "This day will end. How do I want to have spent it?" Then spend the next hour that way.
blogs.seoDescription: Remember you will die, and live better because of it.

blogs.title: Amor Fati: Learning to Love What Happens
blogs.excerpt: Do not just accept fate. Love it. That is the Stoic's hardest — and freest — move.
blogs.content:
# Amor Fati

Amor fati means "love of fate". It goes one step beyond acceptance.

## Acceptance vs love

Acceptance says: "This happened, I will cope." Love says: "This happened, and I will use it."

## Marcus Aurelius on obstacles

Marcus wrote that what stands in the way becomes the way. The obstacle is not a detour from the path — it is the path.

## Practice

When something goes wrong, ask: "What does this make possible that was not possible before?" The answer is often the beginning of the next good thing.
blogs.seoDescription: Do not just accept fate. Love it.

blogs.title: A 10-Minute Stoic Morning Routine That Actually Sticks
blogs.excerpt: No 5 a.m. ice baths. Just three small moves that set the day's frame.
blogs.content:
# A 10-Minute Stoic Morning Routine

## 1. Preview the day (3 minutes)

Think through the day ahead. Where will you be tested? Decide in advance how you will respond.

## 2. Read one passage (4 minutes)

One paragraph from Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, or Epictetus. One idea is enough.

## 3. Write one intention (3 minutes)

One sentence: "Today I will be patient with ___." Carry it in your pocket.

## Why it works

You do not need a perfect morning. You need a morning that reminds you who you want to be before the world tells you otherwise.
blogs.seoDescription: Three small moves that set the day's frame.

blogs.title: Seneca on Anger: Why It Feels Powerful and Leaves You Weaker
blogs.excerpt: Anger promises strength. It delivers regret. Seneca's remedy still works.
blogs.content:
# Seneca on Anger

Seneca wrote a whole book on anger — De Ira — and his verdict is blunt: anger is a brief madness.

## Why anger lies

Anger feels like power because it is loud. But the angry person is not in control; the anger is.

## Seneca's remedy

Delay. When anger rises, do not speak, do not write, do not decide. Give it an hour. Most anger, left alone for an hour, shrinks to a size you can see clearly.

## Practice

Next time you feel the heat rise, say to yourself: "I will answer this in one hour." Then answer it calmly — or not at all.
blogs.seoDescription: Anger promises strength. It delivers regret.

blogs.title: Stoic Journaling: The Evening Review in 5 Minutes
blogs.excerpt: Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself, not for publication. Steal his method.
blogs.content:
# Stoic Journaling

Marcus Aurelius did not write the Meditations for readers. He wrote it for himself, at night, to check his own day.

## The evening review

Three questions, five minutes:

1. What did I do well today?
2. Where did I lose control?
3. What will I do differently tomorrow?

## Why it works

You cannot improve what you never review. The evening review turns every day into a lesson, even the bad ones — especially the bad ones.

## Start tonight

One page. Three questions. No judgement, just honesty.
